title: Emergence of a distinct evolutionary cluster of clade 2.3.4.4b H5 viruses in China during 2024-2025 with rapid evolution and antigenic divergence.
abstract: Clade 2.3.4.4b H5 viruses have undergone continuous evolution since their emergence in China, but the extent of genetic and antigenic diversification among recently circulating viruses remains unclear. Here, we characterized 18 H5 viruses isolated through routine surveillance in China during 2024-2025, together with publicly available clade 2.3.4.4b H5 sequences collected since 2020. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that these isolates formed a distinct evolutionary cluster within clade 2.3.4.4b, designated the G2-derived emerging cluster (G2-EC), which emerged around mid-2024 and exhibited clear genetic divergence from previously circulating H5N1 viruses. G2-EC viruses accumulated a characteristic set of hemagglutinin amino acid substitutions, most of which were located in antigenic regions. Across the clade 2.3.4.4b H5 virus population, the estimated mean HA evolutionary rate was higher during 2024-2025 than during preceding periods. These genetic changes were accompanied by marked antigenic divergence from the Re14 vaccine strain, with 4- to 32-fold reductions in HI titres. Genomic analysis revealed acquisition of PB1 segment from a distinct genetic background in G2-EC H5N1 viruses, followed by the emergence of H5N6 viruses sharing a highly similar genetic backbone but carrying a distinct NA segment, indicating sequential reassortment. Animal experiments showed that representative G2-EC viruses retained high pathogenicity and efficient direct-contact transmission in SPF chickens, while exhibiting relatively limited lethality in mice. Collectively, these findings document a recent evolutionary transition of clade 2.3.4.4b H5 viruses in China, characterized by genetic and antigenic divergence accompanied by sequential reassortment, underscoring the need for continued genomic and antigenic surveillance.

title: Adapting Research Protocols During War: The ANCHOR (Analysis of Network Composition, Health Outcomes, and Resilience) Study.
abstract: Conducting longitudinal infectious disease research during armed conflicts is important for understanding transmission dynamics and preventing outbreaks. War in Ukraine started in 2014, with the escalation to full-scale invasion in 2022, resulting in massive population displacement, infrastructure destruction, mobility restriction for men, and reduced access to healthcare. The ANCHOR (Analysis of Network Composition, Health Outcomes, and Resilience) study, launched in November 2024, examines how war- and displacement-driven changes affect social networks, HIV risks, and HIV care engagement. Here, we report implementation challenges and adaptations as practical lessons that may inform infectious disease surveillance and research in conflict settings. ANCHOR is a cohort study conducted in Kyiv and Lviv in 2024-2026 that enrolled sexual minority men (SMM) using respondent-driven sampling, with 6- and 12-month follow up of participants testing positive for HIV. Data collection included structured behavioral and social network interviews, HIV rapid testing, viral load (VL) assessment, and HIV genetic sequencing. A total of 1,199 SMM were enrolled; of those, 87 tested positive for HIV. Challenges of conducting a research study in an ongoing conflict were identified during the first month of recruitment and prompted protocol revision, incorporating online screening, oral consent, remote interviews, video-assisted HIV self-testing, flexible biospecimen collection. These changes enabled safe completion of study recruitment ahead of the anticipated schedule (within 8 instead of 18 months). Interview follow-up rate was 94% (82/87) at both 6-and 12-month, accompanied by successful biospecimen collection in 61/87 and 45/87 cases at 6-month and 12-month follow-up, respectively. Flexible adaptations in response to the war conditions preserved study integrity and safety of study participants and staff. Availability of various modes of biospecimen collection allowed successful completion of clinical and genomic components of the study, including VL testing and HIV molecular epidemiology analyses despite logistical, infrastructural, and security constraints. Longitudinal biospecimen collection remained challenging due to the ongoing migration and displacement. Lessons from the ANCHOR study can support continuity of infectious disease research in conflict settings and among populations facing barriers to participation. Some of these adaptations may also be applicable to routine infectious disease surveillance, although their utility requires further evaluation.
journal: Journal of epidemiology and global health

title: Molecular insights and phylogenetic context of chicken anemia virus in Tunisian poultry: phylodynamic and phylogeographic perspectives.
abstract: Chicken Anemia Virus (CAV) is an economically important immunosuppressive pathogen in poultry. Despite its global distribution, data on its molecular characteristics and evolutionary behavior in North Africa remain limited. In this study, CAV-positive samples from Tunisian poultry were confirmed by real-time PCR, and complete VP1, VP2, and VP3 coding regions were sequenced. Phylogenetic analysis based on VP1, combined with Bayesian phylodynamic and discrete phylogeographic modeling, was performed to assess viral evolution and dissemination. Tunisian strains exhibited high genetic homogeneity, with 98-100% nucleotide identity in VP1 and full conservation of VP2 and VP3, clustering within genotype II. Phylodynamic analyses indicated that the global CAV ancestor emerged around 1891, followed by a long period of demographic stability and expansion from the 1980s onward. Tunisian sequences formed a distinct cluster with a most recent common ancestor estimated at 1964, suggesting earlier local circulation than inferred from global diffusion patterns. Phylogeographic reconstruction identified China as the principal source of global dispersal and revealed east-to-west transmission pathways, including Taiwan-Egypt and Egypt-Italy. Tunisia appeared in the diffusion network in the late 1970s, with one strongly supported exportation to Italy in 1994, consistent with historical poultry trade. This study provides the first comprehensive evolutionary assessment of CAV in Tunisia, revealing a genetically homogeneous genotype II lineage and highlighting its contribution to Mediterranean viral circulation. The phylodynamic profile underscores historical fluctuations in viral population size that align with global expansion trends, emphasizing the need for strengthened genomic surveillance to capture regional viral movements and anticipate future spread.

title: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective.
abstract: Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security.

title: Environmental stochasticity can account for patterns of within-host respiratory virus evolution.
abstract: The ecological and evolutionary dynamics of populations, including viral populations, are known to be jointly shaped by deterministic and stochastic processes. While the impact of stochastic processes has been rigorously explored for viral dynamics at the level of the host population, most dynamic models for acutely infecting respiratory viral pathogens at the within-host scale remain deterministic in their formulation. Although deterministic formulations may be reasonable for identifying key processes shaping within-host viral population dynamics, recent studies indicate that stochastic processes need to be invoked for understanding patterns of within-host viral evolution. Specifically, several studies have shown that viral allele frequencies can change dramatically over the time course of days in acute infections. Here, we use stochastic dynamic models to explore the role of environmental noise in shaping observed patterns of virus evolution in acute respiratory virus infections. We summarize ways in which environmental stochasticity can be biologically realized in these acute viral infections and describe within-host models that can be implemented to jointly yield viral population dynamics and evolutionary dynamics. We further develop a statistical approach to estimate the extent of environmental noise from observed within-host allele frequency changes, both in the absence and in the presence of additional measurement noise. We test this approach on simulated data and apply it to existing influenza A virus and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 within-host data. With these applications, we show that environmental stochasticity can parsimoniously reproduce key features of empirically observed allele frequency changes. We additionally show that these features differ from those derived under a Wright-Fisher model formulation with a constant effective population size and that the model incorporating environmental stochasticity performs better than the Wright-Fisher model when interfaced with empirical data. Finally, we show that both purifying selection and positive selection can still contribute to within-host viral evolution in the context of environmental noise, providing theoretical support for studies that have found evidence of purifying and positive selection in acutely infecting within-host respiratory virus populations.

title: Phylogeographic Structure in
abstract: Several studies analysed genetic and geographic structuring of plants from the Pacific Northwest of North America and showed a recurring pattern of post-glacial migration from refugia. Willows (Salix) form an important part of the biodiversity of North America. For the genus, a north-to-south migration on the continent was proposed. We studied one North American subclade of six species occurring at the Pacific Coast from California to Alaska with an emphasis on the Sitka willow (Salix sitchensis) to analyse the impact of past geological and climatic events on the spatio-temporal evolution. We utilised RAD sequencing data and biogeographical analyses and revealed a well-supported topology. Based on our results, the common ancestor of the clade originated in the southern Coast Range, and the divergence of S. sitchensis from its sister species Salix lasiolepis and Salix tracyi occurred at 8.04 (3.75-14.85) Ma. Thus, our results showed a south-to-north migration for S. sitchensis, contradicting the pattern observed for the genus. Divergence time estimations gave evidence that S. sitchensis diversified in the Pliocene and therefore predated the Quaternary, but it was the Quaternary period with its climatic fluctuations that shaped the intraspecific diversity patterns. Detailed genetic analyses within the species showed a clear separation of northern and southern populations and suggested that the samples from the north (Alaska) originated from populations in more southern regions. Interestingly, the samples of S. sitchensis from Washington and Canada showed genetic admixture, indicating post-glacial gene flow that connected both edge populations. Our analyses suggest a pre-glacial migration from south to north and a post-glacial migration from northern and southern refugia, with a hybrid zone formation between the populations. Our results offer promising directions for future research and contribute to understanding the bio- and phylogeographical history of western North America.

title: Endemic Cryptococcus gattii Infections, Nova Scotia, Canada, 2016-2024.
abstract: Cryptococcus gattii is poorly characterized in Atlantic Canada. We identified 6 species-confirmed infections in Nova Scotia during 2016-2024. Of those, 5 in western Nova Scotia were genotype VGIIb, including 4 cases without travel outside the province. Previous VGIIb-like detection in a wild animal further supports local acquisition and regional endemicity.

title: Bayesian Inference of Global Land Plant Diversification Dynamics Across the Phanerozoic.
abstract: The patterns and potential drivers of land plant diversification remain puzzling, particularly over deep time and at the global scale. Here, we reconstruct land plant diversification dynamics using an updated time-calibrated phylogeny comprising 30,278 extant species and 39,857 fossil occurrences within the Bayesian birth-death framework. Our analyses indicate that angiosperms exhibit the highest diversification rates, whereas ferns underwent a marked diversification increase during the Cretaceous, coincident with the rapid radiation of angiosperms. Among the major Phanerozoic mass extinctions, the Cretaceous-Paleogene event has the most significant impact on land plant diversity, with estimated genus-level losses of 13%, 14%, and 4% in bryophytes, pteridophytes, and gymnosperms. We also identify a pattern consistent with competitive displacement scenario, in which pteridophyte origination rates declined as gymnosperm diversity increased, accompanying the transition from pteridophyte- to gymnosperm-dominated floras. Plant-insect interactions can be traced to the emergence of pteridophytes, potentially promoting the diversification of pteridophytes and gymnosperms. During the Cretaceous, these associations shift toward angiosperms, as indicated by a positive relationship between insect diversity and angiosperm origination rates. Finally, continental fragmentation, fluctuations in aridity and atmospheric carbon, and sedimentary dynamics show stronger associations with the rise and decline of major land plant groups.

title: Cryptic Invasion and Transmission Dynamics of Peste des Petits Ruminants Virus, Europe, 2024-2026.
abstract: Peste des petits ruminants (PPR) disease has spread in southeastern Europe since July 2024. Virus sequence analyses and field investigations covering 7 countries affected through January 2026 suggest that eastern Romania was the point of introduction and source of regional viral dissemination in the region. Cross-border transmission inferred from genetic data was strongly associated with official records of live animal trade; outbreak investigations indicate additional roles for illegal trade and indirect transmission. Important temporal gaps in the phylogeny suggest that PPR virus has been circulating undetected in multiple areas in southeastern Europe, as noted by the high variability of clinical signs in infected animals. Those findings highlight a real risk for continued spread across Europe. Increased awareness of the difficulty in detecting the disease, coordinated cross-border surveillance, timely data sharing, and integrated control measures are needed to stop the spread of PPR into Europe.

title: Linked deletions in BCP and preS1 enhance HBV replication.
abstract: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) persists as genetically heterogeneous viral populations during chronic infection, yet how linked variants and complementation among coexisting genomes shape viral phenotypes remains unclear. The BCP is a critical transcriptional control element embedded within the X open reading frame and that the preS1 region, aside from encoding a protein domain, controls the transcription of the LHBs protein. We investigated the genomic linkage and cooperative effects of disease-associated BCP and 5' preS1 deletions during chronic HBV infection. Full-length HBV genomes from 246 treatment-naive patients with genotype B and C infection were analyzed by nanopore sequencing. Representative variants were investigated in HepG2 replication, NTCP-dependent infection and hydrodynamic-injection mouse models. Linked BCP-5' preS1 deletions were identified exclusively in genotype C among 3,886 full-length HBV haplotypes and were more prevalent in HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B (Phase II) than in HBeAg-positive chronic HBV infection (Phase I) (26% vs. 9%; p = 0.013). Carriers had higher HBV DNA levels than non-carriers (8.57 ± 0.21 vs. 8.36 ± 0.30 log10 IU/ml; p = 0.028). Linked deletions increased extracellular HBV DNA approximately 8.0-fold relative to WT in transfected HepG2 cells. This replication advantage resulted from complementary effects of increased pgRNA production by BCP deletions and enhanced reverse transcription by the mutant Polymerase generated by the 5' preS1 deletion. However, BCP deletions also impaired productive infection through HBx truncation. HBx supplied in trans restored infectivity in cells and rescued the linked-deletion phenotype in vivo. Distantly linked BCP and 5' preS1 deletions cooperatively enhance HBV replication, revealing how linked variants within heterogeneous HBV populations cooperative to shape viral evolution, persistence, and pathogenicity. HBV mutation studies have traditionally focused on individual genomic regions. However, linked variants within heterogeneous viral populations may exhibit distinct biological and clinical effects. Our findings revealed that low abundance BCP-5' preS1 deletion haplotypes can acquire enhanced replication and infection capacity through intra-genomic cooperation and inter-genomic complementation, highlighting the potential clinical relevance of minority HBV variants. Full-length haplotype based-analyses may uncover previously unrecognized cooperative viral populations that influence persistence and treatment response, warranting validation in larger longitudinal cohorts.

title: Thelazia callipaeda: an emerging zoonotic eyeworm from Asia to Europe and North America.
abstract: Thelazia callipaeda is an emerging zoonotic nematode transmitted by lachryphagous fruit flies to mammalian hosts, including dogs, cats, wild carnivores, and humans, with wildlife reservoirs having a major role in transmission. Once restricted to Asia, the parasite has expanded across many animal species in Europe and, in the past 10 years, in some locations in North America, raising veterinary and public health concerns. Ecological modelling, molecular epidemiology, and entomological findings support ongoing geographical expansion, driven primarily by animal movement and the presence of competent hosts and vectors across regions. Human infections (ie, thelaziasis) primarily present with unilateral conjunctivitis and ocular irritation but can progress to severe ocular disease if left untreated. Increasing reports in domestic and wild animals from newly affected regions, such as the eastern coast of the USA and the Baltic region, highlight the need for integrated surveillance, clinical awareness, molecular monitoring, and coordinated control strategies to mitigate further spread and zoonotic risk. This Review summarises knowledge of the biology, vector ecology, epidemiology, genetic diversity, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of thelaziasis.
